questions.q: Semi-Log Linearization (battery voltage #542): The semi-log values table shows linear relationship between \(x\) and \(\ln y\). Using constant additive rate of change, predict \(\ln y\) at \(x = 4\).
questions.answer: Since \(\ln y\) increases by constant step \(4\) per unit increase in \(x\), at \(x = 4\) we have \(\ln y = 15 + 4 = 19\).

questions.q: Given \(x(t)=3\cos t\) and \(y(t)=3\sin t\), find the point at \(t=\frac{\pi}{3}\), and identify the shape traced by the curve.
questions.answer: \(x\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=3\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=3\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{3}{2}\). \(y\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=3\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=3\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Since \(x^2+y^2=9\cos^2t+9\sin^2t=9\), the curve traces a circle of radius 3 centered at the origin.

questions.q: Eliminate the parameter from \(x(t)=t+1\), \(y(t)=t^2-2\) to find the rectangular equation, and identify the curve.
questions.answer: From \(x=t+1\): \(t=x-1\). Substitute: \(y=(x-1)^2-2=x^2-2x+1-2=x^2-2x-1\). This is a parabola.
questions.explanation: From \(x=t+1\): \(t=x-1\). Substitute: \(y=(x-1)^2-2=x^2-2x+1-2=x^2-2x-1\). This is a parabola.

questions.q: A ball is launched with initial speed 40 m/s at an angle of \(30^\circ\) above horizontal. Its position is modeled by \(x(t)=40\cos(30^\circ)\,t\) and \(y(t)=40\sin(30^\circ)\,t-4.9t^2\). Find the ball's position at \(t=2\) seconds, to one decimal place.
For the same projectile, find the time at which the ball lands (returns to \(y=0\)).
questions.answer: Set \(y(t)=0\): \(20t-4.9t^2=0\), so \(t(20-4.9t)=0\), giving \(t=0\) or \(t=\frac{20}{4.9}\approx4.08\) seconds. The ball lands at \(t\approx4.08\) s.
questions.explanation: Set \(y(t)=0\): \(20t-4.9t^2=0\), so \(t(20-4.9t)=0\), giving \(t=0\) or \(t=\frac{20}{4.9}\approx4.08\) seconds. The ball lands at \(t\approx4.08\) s.

The parametric equations \(x(t)=\cos t\), \(y(t)=\sin t\) trace the full unit circle for \(t\in[0,2\pi)\). Describe the portion of the circle traced when the domain is restricted to \(t\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).
questions.answer: Restricting to \(t\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) traces only the arc from \((1,0)\) (at \(t=0\)) to \((0,1)\) (at \(t=\frac{\pi}{2}\)) — the quarter of the circle lying in Quadrant I.
questions.explanation: Restricting to \(t\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) traces only the arc from \((1,0)\) (at \(t=0\)) to \((0,1)\) (at \(t=\frac{\pi}{2}\)) — the quarter of the circle lying in Quadrant I.

questions.q: Explain why restricting \(t\) in \(x(t)=t^2\), \(y(t)=t\) to \(t\geq0\) changes the rectangular relation from \(x=y^2\) (a full sideways parabola) to only its upper half.
questions.answer: Eliminating the parameter gives \(x=y^2\) for all \(t\), but since \(y=t\) directly, restricting \(t\geq0\) forces \(y\geq0\) as well — so only the upper half of the sideways parabola (where \(y\geq0\)) is actually traced, even though the unrestricted equation \(x=y^2\) would include the lower half too.
questions.explanation: Eliminating the parameter gives \(x=y^2\) for all \(t\), but since \(y=t\) directly, restricting \(t\geq0\) forces \(y\geq0\) as well — so only the upper half of the sideways parabola (where \(y\geq0\)) is actually traced, even though the unrestricted equation \(x=y^2\) would include the lower half too.

questions.q: A point moves along a circle of radius 4 according to \(x(t)=4\cos\left(t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\), \(y(t)=4\sin\left(t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\). Find its position at \(t=0\), and explain the effect of the \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) phase shift compared to \(x(t)=4\cos t\), \(y(t)=4\sin t\).
questions.target: Parametric equations for circular motion with a phase shift
questions.answer: At \(t=0\): \(x(0)=4\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)=2\sqrt{2}\), \(y(0)=4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=2\sqrt{2}\). Without the phase shift, the point would start at \((4,0)\) when \(t=0\); the added \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) advances the starting position by an eighth of a full revolution counterclockwise, to \((2\sqrt{2},2\sqrt{2})\), while the circle traced and the speed of travel remain unchanged.
questions.explanation: At \(t=0\): \(x(0)=4\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)=2\sqrt{2}\), \(y(0)=4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=2\sqrt{2}\). Without the phase shift, the point would start at \((4,0)\) when \(t=0\); the added \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) advances the starting position by an eighth of a full revolution counterclockwise, to \((2\sqrt{2},2\sqrt{2})\), while the circle traced and the speed of travel remain unchanged.

questions.q: Eliminate the parameter to determine the Cartesian equation of the curve \(x = 1 + 2\sec t\), \(y = -2 + 3\tan t\). State the shape, center, and vertices.
questions.answer: Isolate the trigonometric terms: \(\sec t = \frac{x - 1}{2}, \qquad \tan t = \frac{y + 2}{3}.\) Apply the fundamental Pythagorean identity \(\sec^2 t - \tan^2 t = 1\): \(\left(\frac{x - 1}{2}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{y + 2}{3}\right)^2 = 1 \Rightarrow \frac{(x - 1)^2}{4} - \frac{(y + 2)^2}{9} = 1.\) This is a horizontal hyperbola with:Center: \((h, k) = (1, -2)\)Transverse semi-axis: \(a = 2\)Vertices: \((h \pm a, k) = (1 \pm 2, -2) = (-1, -2)\) and \((3, -2)\)
questions.explanation: Isolate the trigonometric terms: \(\sec t = \frac{x - 1}{2}, \qquad \tan t = \frac{y + 2}{3}.\) Apply the fundamental Pythagorean identity \(\sec^2 t - \tan^2 t = 1\): \(\left(\frac{x - 1}{2}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{y + 2}{3}\right)^2 = 1 \Rightarrow \frac{(x - 1)^2}{4} - \frac{(y + 2)^2}{9} = 1.\) This is a horizontal hyperbola with:Center: \((h, k) = (1, -2)\)Transverse semi-axis: \(a = 2\)Vertices: \((h \pm a, k) = (1 \pm 2, -2) = (-1, -2)\) and \((3, -2)\)

questions.q: Given vectors \(\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j}\) and \(\mathbf{b} = -3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}\), find the scalar projection of \(\mathbf{a}\) onto \(\mathbf{b}\) and the angle \(\theta\) between them to the nearest tenth of a degree.
questions.answer: Calculate the dot product: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = (2)(-3) + (-5)(4) = -6 - 20 = -26.\) Calculate the magnitudes: \(|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-5)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 25} = \sqrt{29} \approx 5.385,\) \(|\mathbf{b}| = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5.\) Scalar projection of \(\mathbf{a}\) onto \(\mathbf{b}\): \(\mathrm{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{b}|} = \frac{-26}{5} = -5.2.\) Angle \(\theta\) between vectors: \(\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|} = \frac{-26}{5\sqrt{29}} \approx -0.9656 \Rightarrow \theta = \arccos(-0.9656) \approx 164.9°.\)
questions.explanation: Calculate the dot product: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = (2)(-3) + (-5)(4) = -6 - 20 = -26.\) Calculate the magnitudes: \(|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-5)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 25} = \sqrt{29} \approx 5.385,\) \(|\mathbf{b}| = \sqrt{(-3)^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5.\) Scalar projection of \(\mathbf{a}\) onto \(\mathbf{b}\): \(\mathrm{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{b}|} = \frac{-26}{5} = -5.2.\) Angle \(\theta\) between vectors: \(\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|} = \frac{-26}{5\sqrt{29}} \approx -0.9656 \Rightarrow \theta = \arccos(-0.9656) \approx 164.9°.\)

questions.q: Decompose the vector \(\mathbf{u} = \langle 6, 2 \rangle\) into components parallel and orthogonal to \(\mathbf{v} = \langle 3, 4 \rangle\).
questions.answer: Step 1: Compute dot product and squared magnitude: \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = (6)(3) + (2)(4) = 18 + 8 = 26.\) \(||\mathbf{v}||^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25.\) Step 2: Vector projection (parallel component): \(\mathbf{u}_\parallel = \mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{||\mathbf{v}||^2}\right)\mathbf{v} = \frac{26}{25}\langle 3, 4 \rangle = \left\langle \frac{78}{25}, \frac{104}{25} \right\rangle = \langle 3.12, 4.16 \rangle.\) Step 3: Orthogonal component: \(\mathbf{u}_\perp = \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_\parallel = \langle 6 - 3.12, 2 - 4.16 \rangle = \langle 2.88, -2.16 \rangle = \left\langle \frac{72}{25}, -\frac{54}{25} \right\rangle.\) Check: \(\mathbf{u}_\perp \cdot \mathbf{v} = (2.88)(3) + (-2.16)(4) = 8.64 - 8.64 = 0\). \(\checkmark\)
questions.explanation: Step 1: Compute dot product and squared magnitude: \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = (6)(3) + (2)(4) = 18 + 8 = 26.\) \(||\mathbf{v}||^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25.\) Step 2: Vector projection (parallel component): \(\mathbf{u}_\parallel = \mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{||\mathbf{v}||^2}\right)\mathbf{v} = \frac{26}{25}\langle 3, 4 \rangle = \left\langle \frac{78}{25}, \frac{104}{25} \right\rangle = \langle 3.12, 4.16 \rangle.\) Step 3: Orthogonal component: \(\mathbf{u}_\perp = \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_\parallel = \langle 6 - 3.12, 2 - 4.16 \rangle = \langle 2.88, -2.16 \rangle = \left\langle \frac{72}{25}, -\frac{54}{25} \right\rangle.\) Check: \(\mathbf{u}_\perp \cdot \mathbf{v} = (2.88)(3) + (-2.16)(4) = 8.64 - 8.64 = 0\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.q: A right circular cone has a base radius of 6 cm and a slant height of 10 cm. Find (a) its perpendicular vertical height \(h\), (b) its volume \(V\) in terms of \(\pi\), and (c) its total surface area in terms of \(\pi\).
questions.answer: (a) Vertical height: Using the Pythagorean relation \(l^2 = r^2 + h^2\): \(h = \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{100 - 36} = \sqrt{64} = \mathbf{8\mathrm{\ cm}}\) (b) Volume: \(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \frac{1}{3}\pi (6^2)(8) = \frac{1}{3}\pi (36)(8) = 12 \times 8\pi = \mathbf{96\pi\mathrm{\ cm}^3} \approx 301.59\mathrm{\ cm}^3\) (c) Total surface area: \(\mathrm{TSA} = \pi r^2 + \pi r l = \pi (6^2) + \pi(6)(10) = 36\pi + 60\pi = \mathbf{96\pi\mathrm{\ cm}^2} \approx 301.59\mathrm{\ cm}^2\)
questions.explanation: (a) Vertical height: Using the Pythagorean relation \(l^2 = r^2 + h^2\): \(h = \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{100 - 36} = \sqrt{64} = \mathbf{8\mathrm{\ cm}}\) (b) Volume: \(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \frac{1}{3}\pi (6^2)(8) = \frac{1}{3}\pi (36)(8) = 12 \times 8\pi = \mathbf{96\pi\mathrm{\ cm}^3} \approx 301.59\mathrm{\ cm}^3\) (c) Total surface area: \(\mathrm{TSA} = \pi r^2 + \pi r l = \pi (6^2) + \pi(6)(10) = 36\pi + 60\pi = \mathbf{96\pi\mathrm{\ cm}^2} \approx 301.59\mathrm{\ cm}^2\)

questions.q: Two particles, A and B, move in the xy-plane. Their position vectors at time \(t\) seconds, for \(t \geq 0\), are given by \(\mathbf{r}_A(t) = \left(2t ; 4t - 1\right)\) and \(\mathbf{r}_B(t) = \left(3 + 5t ; 1 - 2t\right)\) respectively. The particles start their motion at \(t=0\). Find the minimum distance between particle A and particle B.
questions.target: Parametric equations for lines and conics
questions.answer: The position vectors of particle A and particle B at time \(t\) are given by \(\mathbf{r}_A(t) = \left(2t ; 4t - 1\right)\) and \(\mathbf{r}_B(t) = \left(3 + 5t ; 1 - 2t\right)\). The vector representing the displacement from particle B to particle A at time \(t\) is \(\mathbf{d}(t) = \mathbf{r}_A(t) - \mathbf{r}_B(t) = \left(2t - (3 + 5t) ; (4t - 1) - (1 - 2t)\right) = \left(-3t - 3 ; 6t - 2\right)\). The distance between the particles at time \(t\) is the magnitude of this displacement vector, \(D(t) = ||\mathbf{d}(t)|| = \sqrt{(-3t - 3)^2 + (6t - 2)^2}\). To minimize the distance, we can minimize the square of the distance, \(D(t)^2 = (-3t - 3)^2 + (6t - 2)^2\). Let \(f(t) = D(t)^2 = (9t^2 + 18t + 9) + (36t^2 - 24t + 4) = 45t^2 - 6t + 13\). This is a quadratic function of \(t\), representing a parabola opening upwards. The minimum value occurs at the vertex. The t-coordinate of the vertex is given by \(t = -\frac{b}{2a}\), where \(a=45\) and \(b=-6\). So, \(t = -\frac{-6}{2 \times 45} = \frac{6}{90} = \frac{1}{15}\). Now, substitute this value of \(t\) back into the expression for \(D(t)^2\) to find the minimum squared distance: \(f(\frac{1}{15}) = 45(\frac{1}{15})^2 - 6(\frac{1}{15}) + 13 = 45(\frac{1}{225}) - \frac{6}{15} + 13 = \frac{1}{5} - \frac{2}{5} + 13 = -\frac{1}{5} + 13 = \frac{-1 + 65}{5} = \frac{64}{5}\). The minimum distance is the square root of the minimum squared distance: \(D_{min} = \sqrt{\frac{64}{5}} = \frac{8}{\sqrt{5}} = \frac{8\sqrt{5}}{5}\).
questions.explanation: The position vectors of particle A and particle B at time \(t\) are given by \(\mathbf{r}_A(t) = \left(2t ; 4t - 1\right)\) and \(\mathbf{r}_B(t) = \left(3 + 5t ; 1 - 2t\right)\). The vector representing the displacement from particle B to particle A at time \(t\) is \(\mathbf{d}(t) = \mathbf{r}_A(t) - \mathbf{r}_B(t) = \left(2t - (3 + 5t) ; (4t - 1) - (1 - 2t)\right) = \left(-3t - 3 ; 6t - 2\right)\). The distance between the particles at time \(t\) is the magnitude of this displacement vector, \(D(t) = ||\mathbf{d}(t)|| = \sqrt{(-3t - 3)^2 + (6t - 2)^2}\). To minimize the distance, we can minimize the square of the distance, \(D(t)^2 = (-3t - 3)^2 + (6t - 2)^2\). Let \(f(t) = D(t)^2 = (9t^2 + 18t + 9) + (36t^2 - 24t + 4) = 45t^2 - 6t + 13\). This is a quadratic function of \(t\), representing a parabola opening upwards. The minimum value occurs at the vertex. The t-coordinate of the vertex is given by \(t = -\frac{b}{2a}\), where \(a=45\) and \(b=-6\). So, \(t = -\frac{-6}{2 \times 45} = \frac{6}{90} = \frac{1}{15}\). Now, substitute this value of \(t\) back into the expression for \(D(t)^2\) to find the minimum squared distance: \(f(\frac{1}{15}) = 45(\frac{1}{15})^2 - 6(\frac{1}{15}) + 13 = 45(\frac{1}{225}) - \frac{6}{15} + 13 = \frac{1}{5} - \frac{2}{5} + 13 = -\frac{1}{5} + 13 = \frac{-1 + 65}{5} = \frac{64}{5}\). The minimum distance is the square root of the minimum squared distance: \(D_{min} = \sqrt{\frac{64}{5}} = \frac{8}{\sqrt{5}} = \frac{8\sqrt{5}}{5}\).

questions.q: Two vectors are given by \(\vec{u} = 3\hat{i} + k\hat{j}\) and \(\vec{v} = -\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}\). If \(\vec{u}\) and \(\vec{v}\) are orthogonal, find the value of the scalar parameter \(k\).
questions.answer: Two vectors \(\vec{u}\) and \(\vec{v}\) are orthogonal if and only if their dot product is zero. The dot product of \(\vec{u} = u_1\hat{i} + u_2\hat{j}\) and \(\vec{v} = v_1\hat{i} + v_2\hat{j}\) is given by \(\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2\). Given \(\vec{u} = 3\hat{i} + k\hat{j}\) and \(\vec{v} = -\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}\), their dot product is: \(\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = (3)(-1) + (k)(4)\) \(\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = -3 + 4k\) For the vectors to be orthogonal, their dot product must be zero: \(-3 + 4k = 0\) \(4k = 3\) \(k = \frac{3}{4}\)

questions.answer: To find the component form of a vector \(\vec{PQ}\) from point \(P(x_1, y_1)\) to point \(Q(x_2, y_2)\), we subtract the coordinates of the initial point \(P\) from the coordinates of the terminal point \(Q\). questions.q: Exponential Function Graph (pendulum swing #567): Using the plotted exponential function \(g(x) = 5\cdot 2^x + 1\) with horizontal asymptote \(y = 1\), evaluate \(g(2)\).
questions.target: Parametric equations for lines and conics
questions.explanation: We solve the problem by synthesizing Vieta's formulas with the geometric properties of complex numbers. **Step 1: Condition for an Equilateral Triangle with the Origin** In the complex plane, three points \(0\), \(z_1\), and \(z_2\) form the vertices of an equilateral triangle if and only if one non-zero vertex is obtained by rotating the other about the origin by \(\pm \frac{\pi}{3}\): \(\frac{z_2}{z_1} = e^{\pm i\pi/3} = \frac{1 \pm i\sqrt{3}}{2}\) This is equivalent to the quadratic in \(\frac{z_2}{z_1}\): \(\left(\frac{z_2}{z_1}\right)^2 - \frac{z_2}{z_1} + 1 = 0 \Leftrightarrow z_1^2 - z_1 z_2 + z_2^2 = 0\) Rewriting in terms of the elementary symmetric polynomials \(z_1 + z_2\) and \(z_1 z_2\): \((z_1 + z_2)^2 - 3z_1 z_2 = 0\) **Step 2: Apply Vieta's Formulas** From the given equation \(z^2 - 2mz + (m^2 + 3m - 6) = 0\): \(z_1 + z_2 = 2m\) \(z_1 z_2 = m^2 + 3m - 6\) Substituting these into the equilateral condition: \((2m)^2 - 3(m^2 + 3m - 6) = 0\) \(4m^2 - 3m^2 - 9m + 18 = 0\) \(m^2 - 9m + 18 = 0\) Factoring gives: \((m - 3)(m - 6) = 0 \Rightarrow m = 3 \quad \mathrm{or} \quad m = 6\) **Step 3: Verify the Roots are Non-Real (Non-Degenerate Triangle)** The discriminant of the quadratic in \(z\) is: \(\Delta = (-2m)^2 - 4(1)(m^2 + 3m - 6) = 4m^2 - 4m^2 - 12m + 24 = 24 - 12m\) For \(m = 3\), \(\Delta = 24 - 36 = -12 < 0\), so the roots are distinct non-real complex numbers. For \(m = 6\), \(\Delta = 24 - 72 = -48 < 0\), so the roots are also distinct non-real complex numbers. Thus, both values yield valid, non-degenerate triangles. **Step 4: Compute the Areas of the Triangles** Because the origin is a vertex of each equilateral triangle, the side length \(s\) satisfies: \(s^2 = |z_1 - 0|^2 = |z_1|^2 = z_1 \overline{z_1}\) Since the coefficients of the quadratic in \(z\) are real and the roots are non-real, \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) are complex conjugates (\(z_2 = \overline{z_1}\)). Thus: \(s^2 = z_1 z_2 = m^2 + 3m - 6\) The area of an equilateral triangle with side length \(s\) is: \(\mathrm{Area} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} s^2 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(m^2 + 3m - 6)\) - For \(m = 3\): \(s_1^2 = 3^2 + 3(3) - 6 = 12 \Rightarrow \mathrm{Area}_1 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(12) = 3\sqrt{3}\) - For \(m = 6\): \(s_2^2 = 6^2 + 3(6) - 6 = 48 \Rightarrow \mathrm{Area}_2 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(48) = 12\sqrt{3}\) The sum of the possible areas is: \(3\sqrt{3} + 12\sqrt{3} = 15\sqrt{3}\) **Common Misconceptions:** - Choice B (\(12\sqrt{3}\)) considers only the maximum area from \(m = 6\), failing to sum both valid configurations. - Choice C (\(\frac{15\sqrt{3}}{2}\)) occurs if one calculates the area using \(\frac{1}{2} b h\) with base \(b = \mathrm{Im}(z_1) = \sqrt{3m-6}\) instead of the full segment \(|z_1 - z_2| = 2\sqrt{3m-6}\). - Choice D (\(9\sqrt{3}\)) results from an arithmetic error when evaluating \(s^2\) or confusing the side length with the real part \(m\).

questions.q: Consider the system of linear equations represented by the matrix equation \(\left(1, 1, 1 ; 1, 2, 3 ; 3, 5, k\right) \left(x ; y ; z\right) = \left(6 ; 14 ; m\right)\) where \(k\) and \(m\) are real constants. Suppose the system is consistent and has infinitely many solutions. Let \(P(x, y, z)\) be the unique solution that minimizes the squared Euclidean distance from the origin, \(d^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2\). What is the value of \(k + m + d^2\)?
questions.answer: We solve the problem in three main stages: 1. **Determine the parameter \(k\):** For the system to have infinitely many solutions, the coefficient matrix must be singular (its determinant must be zero): \(\det \left(1, 1, 1 ; 1, 2, 3 ; 3, 5, k\right) = 1(2k - 15) - 1(k - 9) + 1(5 - 6) = k - 7\) Setting \(k - 7 = 0\) yields \(k = 7\). 2. **Determine the parameter \(m\):** Set up the augmented matrix with \(k = 7\) and perform Gaussian elimination: \(\left(1, 1, 1, 6 ; 1, 2, 3, 14 ; 3, 5, 7, m\right) \rightarrow \left(1, 1, 1, 6 ; 0, 1, 2, 8 ; 0, 2, 4, m - 18\right) \rightarrow \left(1, 1, 1, 6 ; 0, 1, 2, 8 ; 0, 0, 0, m - 34\right)\) For the system to be consistent, the bottom row must be all zeros, which requires \(m - 34 = 0 \Rightarrow m = 34\). 3. **Parametrize the solution and minimize \(d^2\):** From row 2: \(y + 2z = 8 \Rightarrow y = 8 - 2z\). From row 1: \(x + (8 - 2z) + z = 6 \Rightarrow x = z - 2\). Letting \(z = t\), any solution has the form \((x, y, z) = (t - 2, 8 - 2t, t)\). The squared distance to the origin is: \(d^2(t) = (t - 2)^2 + (8 - 2t)^2 + t^2 = (t^2 - 4t + 4) + (4t^2 - 32t + 64) + t^2 = 6t^2 - 36t + 68\) This quadratic reaches its minimum at the vertex: \(t = -\frac{-36}{2(6)} = 3\) Evaluating \(d^2\) at \(t = 3\): \(d^2(3) = 6(3)^2 - 36(3) + 68 = 54 - 108 + 68 = 14\) (Corresponding to the point \((1, 2, 3)\), where \(1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 = 14\)). 4. **Calculate \(k + m + d^2\):** \(k + m + d^2 = 7 + 34 + 14 = 55\) **Common Misconceptions:** - Choice B (47) adds \(x_0 + y_0 + z_0 = 6\) instead of \(d^2 = 14\). - Choice C (38) mistakenly assumes row 3 is the direct sum of row 1 and row 2, yielding \(k = 4, m = 20\). - Choice D (109) miscalculates the vertex using \(t = -b/a = 6\), which gives \(d^2 = 68\).

From row 1: \(x + (8 - 2z) + z = 6 \Rightarrow x = z - 2\). Letting \(z = t\), any solution has the form \((x, y, z) = (t - 2, 8 - 2t, t)\). The squared distance to the origin is: \(d^2(t) = (t - 2)^2 + (8 - 2t)^2 + t^2 = (t^2 - 4t + 4) + (4t^2 - 32t + 64) + t^2 = 6t^2 - 36t + 68\) This quadratic reaches its minimum at the vertex: \(t = -\frac{-36}{2(6)} = 3\) Evaluating \(d^2\) at \(t = 3\): \(d^2(3) = 6(3)^2 - 36(3) + 68 = 54 - 108 + 68 = 14\) (Corresponding to the point \((1, 2, 3)\), where \(1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 = 14\)). 4. **Calculate \(k + m + d^2\):** \(k + m + d^2 = 7 + 34 + 14 = 55\) **Common Misconceptions:** - Choice B (47) adds \(x_0 + y_0 + z_0 = 6\) instead of \(d^2 = 14\). - Choice C (38) mistakenly assumes row 3 is the direct sum of row 1 and row 2, yielding \(k = 4, m = 20\). - Choice D (109) miscalculates the vertex using \(t = -b/a = 6\), which gives \(d^2 = 68\).

questions.q: Semi-Log Linearization (fluid pressure #568): The semi-log values table shows linear relationship between \(x\) and \(\ln y\). Using constant additive rate of change, predict \(\ln y\) at \(x = 4\).
questions.answer: Since \(\ln y\) increases by constant step \(2\) per unit increase in \(x\), at \(x = 4\) we have \(\ln y = 10 + 2 = 12\).
questions.explanation: We can solve this system using algebraic expansion or complex numbers. **Method 1: Squaring and Adding** Square both equations and add them together: \((x^3 - 3xy^2)^2 + (3x^2y - y^3)^2 = 10^2 + 5^2 = 100 + 25 = 125\) Expanding the left-hand side: \((x^6 - 6x^4y^2 + 9x^2y^4) + (9x^4y^2 - 6x^2y^4 + y^6) = x^6 + 3x^4y^2 + 3x^2y^4 + y^6\) Notice that this expression is the binomial expansion of \((x^2 + y^2)^3\): \((x^2 + y^2)^3 = 125\) Taking the real cube root of both sides gives: \(x^2 + y^2 = \sqrt[3]{125} = 5\) **Method 2: Complex Numbers** Let \(z = x + iy\). By De Moivre's formula / binomial expansion: \(z^3 = (x + iy)^3 = (x^3 - 3xy^2) + i(3x^2y - y^3) = 10 + 5i\) Taking the modulus of both sides: \(|z^3| = |z|^3 = |10 + 5i| = \sqrt{10^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{125} = 5\sqrt{5}\) Since \(|z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\), we have: \((x^2 + y^2)^{3/2} = 5^{3/2} \Rightarrow x^2 + y^2 = 5\) **Misconception Traps:** - Choice C, \(5\sqrt{5}\), occurs if one incorrectly assumes the sum of squares yields \((x^2 + y^2)^2\) instead of \((x^2 + y^2)^3\), computing \(\sqrt{125}\). - Choice D, \(25\), arises from mistakenly dividing \(125\) by \(5\) rather than taking the cube root. - Choice A, \(\sqrt{5}\), results from erroneously taking the fourth root or an extra square root.

questions.q: In the system of linear equations below, \(k\) is a real constant. \((k - 1)x + 6y, = 18 ; 2x + ky, = 12\) For which value of \(k\) does the system have infinitely many solutions \((x, y)\)?
questions.target: Parametric equations for circular motion with a phase shift
questions.answer: For a system of two linear equations in two variables to have infinitely many solutions, the two equations must represent the exact same line. This requires the ratios of the corresponding coefficients and the constant terms to all be equal: \(\frac{k - 1}{2} = \frac{6}{k} = \frac{18}{12}\) First, simplify the ratio of the constant terms: \(\frac{18}{12} = \frac{3}{2}\) Next, set the ratio of the \(y\)-coefficients equal to \(\frac{3}{2}\): \(\frac{6}{k} = \frac{3}{2} \Rightarrow 3k = 12 \Rightarrow k = 4\) Verify this value by checking the ratio of the \(x\)-coefficients when \(k = 4\): \(\frac{4 - 1}{2} = \frac{3}{2}\) All three ratios are equal to \(\frac{3}{2}\), which confirms that both equations describe the line \(x + 2y = 6\). Common error trap: Setting the determinant of the coefficient matrix to zero yields \(k(k - 1) - 12 = 0\), or \(k^2 - k - 12 = (k - 4)(k + 3) = 0\). Choosing \(k = -3\) is incorrect because for \(k = -3\), the lines have equal slopes (\(-2\)) but different constant ratios (\(-2 eq \frac{3}{2}\)), meaning the system has no solution rather than infinitely many.
questions.explanation: For a system of two linear equations in two variables to have infinitely many solutions, the two equations must represent the exact same line. This requires the ratios of the corresponding coefficients and the constant terms to all be equal: \(\frac{k - 1}{2} = \frac{6}{k} = \frac{18}{12}\) First, simplify the ratio of the constant terms: \(\frac{18}{12} = \frac{3}{2}\) Next, set the ratio of the \(y\)-coefficients equal to \(\frac{3}{2}\): \(\frac{6}{k} = \frac{3}{2} \Rightarrow 3k = 12 \Rightarrow k = 4\) Verify this value by checking the ratio of the \(x\)-coefficients when \(k = 4\): \(\frac{4 - 1}{2} = \frac{3}{2}\) All three ratios are equal to \(\frac{3}{2}\), which confirms that both equations describe the line \(x + 2y = 6\). Common error trap: Setting the determinant of the coefficient matrix to zero yields \(k(k - 1) - 12 = 0\), or \(k^2 - k - 12 = (k - 4)(k + 3) = 0\). Choosing \(k = -3\) is incorrect because for \(k = -3\), the lines have equal slopes (\(-2\)) but different constant ratios (\(-2 eq \frac{3}{2}\)), meaning the system has no solution rather than infinitely many.
